strengths: The orientation-resolved analysis reveals structured generalization patterns that average accuracy would obscure. These findings have an identifiable audience in visual robustness, representation learning, and computational neuroscience.

The experimental coverage is substantial: three object categories, multiple training-orientation ranges, several architectures, cross-category transfer, and controls involving pretraining, augmentation, and dataset size. Five repetitions and a fixed total training-image budget strengthen the descriptive evidence.

The small-angle, in-plane, and silhouette components provide an interpretable account of the observed accuracy patterns. The reported correlations and component comparisons support their usefulness as descriptive models.
The experimental paradigm is understandable, and the heatmaps connect quantitative results to recognizable object views. Code and data links are provided.
weaknesses: Necessary: The mechanistic conclusions exceed the evidence. Figures 5b–c establish correlations between accuracy and activation similarity, and between fully-seen and partially-seen instances. They do not establish that particular shared features causally transmit invariance between these groups; common image geometry and joint training remain alternative explanations. Sections 3.3–4 should consistently present dissemination as a supported hypothesis, or provide targeted interventions with appropriate controls. The concluding assertion that biological recognition mechanisms largely apply to DNNs also needs narrower wording.

Necessary: Predictive validation is not established separately from fitting. Section 2.4 optimizes the logistic parameters directly against network accuracy using Pearson correlation, and Figure 4 reports that same statistic without describing a held-out evaluation for this fitted model. The high correlations therefore demonstrate goodness of fit, but do not establish prediction for unseen measurements or experimental settings. Specify the fitting/evaluation protocol and either provide held-out validation or restrict the claims to descriptive characterization.

Necessary: The generalizable/non-generalizable partition needs a mathematically consistent specification. Section 2.5 thresholds f_w at 10% of its maximum, although Equation 4 sums four logistic outputs and optimizes only correlation. Pearson correlation is unchanged by an additive offset, whereas this threshold is not. Figure S9c displays scores around 1.8–2.4, which would all exceed 10% of their maximum without another transformation. Clarify any normalization, reconcile the figure with the stated rule, and demonstrate partition stability. This matters because the partition underlies the subsequent neural analyses.

Necessary: The invariance metric requires validation for its interpretation. Equations 5–6 compare means across orientation sets, so equal means can conceal strongly view-dependent responses. Equation 7 additionally excludes pairs when either mean falls below the activity threshold, including potentially informative losses of response. Report the retained counts L and check whether the conclusions survive orientation-level comparisons and reasonable threshold changes; otherwise describe the quantity more narrowly as similarity of selected mean activations.

Optional: Keeping a fixed partially-seen evaluation cohort while independently varying fully-seen diversity and its image budget would better isolate the sources of improvement. Larger labels in the dense summary figures and fuller reporting of orientation sampling, discretization, and evaluation-set sizes would also improve usability.
